activities.title: Python — 01 Output
activities.description: Everything print() can do: strings, variables, both together, joining with +, tabs and blank lines, and formatted numbers. Six Parsons problems and an MCQ. No loops and no conditions yet, so nothing here is indented — the whole job is order.

config.title: Print a menu
config.instructions: Put the four lines in the order the menu should appear on screen. Nothing is indented in this activity — every line starts at the left.

key.explanation: Python runs the lines from top to bottom, one after another, so the order you write the print statements in is exactly the order they appear on screen.

check.stdout:
MAIN MENU
1. New game
2. Load game
3. Quit

config.title: Print strings and variables together
config.instructions: A variable has to be given its value before anything can print it. Put the lines in an order where that is always true.

lines.text: print("Next year she will be", age + 1)

key.explanation: print() can take several things at once, separated by commas, and it puts a space between them for you. The comma also lets you mix a string and a number without converting anything. Move either print above the line that creates the variable it uses and Python stops with a NameError.

check.stdout:
Name: Aoife
Age: 17
Next year she will be 18

config.title: Join strings with +
config.instructions: Build a full name out of two separate strings. Three of these lines are wrong — one of them looks almost right.

key.explanation: + glues strings together exactly as they are, so the space between the names has to be put there on purpose — first + last would give "AdaLovelace". + only works between two strings: "Letters:" + len(full) tries to add a number to a string and stops with a TypeError, which is why the last line uses a comma instead.

config.title: Tabs and blank lines
config.instructions: Lay out a small price list in columns. \t is a tab and \n is a new line — both go inside the quotes.

key.explanation:
is one tab character, so the columns line up however long the words are — two spaces typed by hand would not. 
 starts a new line, so "
Thank you" leaves a blank line above the message. 
 in the middle of the heading would split it over two lines instead of making two columns.

check.stdout:
Report
======
Item	Price
Tea	1.50
Coffee	2.00

Thank you

config.title: Formatting numbers in a print
config.instructions: Print prices to exactly two decimal places using an f-string. Watch the f — one of the wrong lines is missing it.

key.explanation: The f before the opening quote is what makes Python look inside the { }. Without it the line prints the curly brackets literally. :.2f means "two digits after the point", which is what turns 7.5 into 7.50; :2f without the dot means something else entirely. The total has to be worked out before the line that prints it.

steps.title: A receipt, putting it all together

config.title: A receipt, putting it all together
config.instructions: Everything from this section at once: variables, a repeated string, a tab, a formatted price and a blank line.

key.explanation: "-" * len(shop) repeats the dash once per character, so the underline is always exactly as wide as the name. Multiplying a string by another string is meaningless and stops the program. price is a number, so it cannot be joined with + — an f-string handles the mixing, and :.2f is what keeps the trailing zero on a price like 3.70.

check.stdout:
Nybble Cafe
-----------
Latte	€3.75

Thank you for your visit

config.title: print() — the details
config.instructions: Five questions on what print() does with commas, plus signs and escape characters.

options.text: An error, because you cannot print a string and a number together

questions.stem: Which line stops the program with a TypeError?
What does \t do inside a string?

options.text: Inserts a tab, so text after it lines up in a column
Prints the two characters backslash and t

questions.stem: How many lines does this print in total, counting the blank one?

q1.explanation: A comma inside print() separates two things to print and puts a single space between them. It also means the number never has to be converted.

q2.explanation: Both of those are strings, not numbers — the quotes make them text. + on two strings joins them, giving 53.

q3.explanation: + cannot join a string to a number. str(17) turns it into text first, a comma sidesteps the problem, and an f-string does the conversion for you.

q4.explanation: \t is a single tab character. It moves to the next tab stop, so columns line up no matter how long the words are — typed spaces would not.

q5.explanation: "One" is one line, the \n makes a blank line, and "Two" is the third.
